introduction: Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21–34, Socrates’ retelling of Prodicus’ Choice of Heracles. Read this controlled course adaptation with the glosses, then revisit its source and historical setting on page three.

This is an allegory attributed to Prodicus within Xenophon’s Socratic dialogue. The speeches are drastically shortened and newly worded. The reader’s final question is supplied; no historical meeting is asserted.
Demonstratives and questions distinguish two speakers, their promises, and the paths they recommend.

paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Ἡρακλῆς νέος ὢν ἐν ἡσυχίᾳ ἐκάθητο. περὶ τοῦ βίου ἐσκόπει· ποτέραν ὁδὸν αἱρήσεται; δύο γυναῖκες προσῆλθον. ἡ μὲν Ἀρετὴ ἦν, ἡ δὲ Κακία.
Ἡ Κακία πρώτη λέγει· «ἥδε ἡ ὁδὸς ἡδεῖά ἐστιν. δεῦρο ἐλθέ. ἐνταῦθα σῖτον καὶ ποτὸν εὑρήσεις. οὐ πολλοὺς πόνους ἕξεις.»
«Τίνες τὸν σῖτον παρασκευάζουσιν; πόθεν τὰ χρήματα;» ταύτας τὰς ἐρωτήσεις ὁ ἀναγινώσκων νῦν ἐρωτᾷ. ἡ μὲν ἐπαγγελία ἡδεῖά ἐστιν· ἡ δὲ ἐργασία τίνος;
Ἡ δὲ Ἀρετὴ λέγει· «ἐκείνη ἡ ὁδὸς ἄλλην ἐλπίδα παρέχει. οὐδὲν τῶν καλῶν ἄνευ πόνου οἱ θεοὶ διδόασιν. τοῖς φίλοις βοήθει καὶ τὰ καλὰ πράττε.»
Ἑκατέρα γυνὴ περὶ εὐδαιμονίας λέγει. ἡ μὲν τὴν νῦν ἡδονὴν δεικνύει, ἡ δὲ τὸν ἔπειτα βίον. οὐ πᾶσα ἡδονὴ κακή· τίς δὲ ἡδονὴ τοὺς φίλους βλάπτει;
Οὗτος ὁ μῦθος οὐχ ἱστορία μάχης ἐστίν. πρόκεινται δύο βίοι. τίνα βίον θαυμάζεις; πῶς κρίνεις τὰς ἐπαγγελίας; ἡ καλὴ ὄψις οὐ μόνη τὴν ἀλήθειαν δηλοῖ.

reading.translation:
Heracles, when young, was sitting in a quiet place. He was considering his life: which of two roads will he choose? Two women approached. One was Virtue, the other Vice.

Vice speaks first: “This road here is pleasant. Come here. Here you will find food and drink. You will not have many toils.”

“Who prepares the food? Where do the resources come from?” The reader now asks these questions. The promise is pleasant; but whose is the work?

Virtue says, “That road offers a different hope. The gods give none of the fine things without toil. Help your friends and do noble things.”

Each woman speaks about happiness. One shows present pleasure, the other life afterwards. Not every pleasure is bad; but which pleasure harms friends?

This story is not an account of a battle. Two ways of life lie before us. Which life do you admire? How do you judge the promises? A fine appearance does not by itself reveal the truth.

blocks.title: ἀρετή and κακία: abstract ideas as characters
body: ἀρετή can mean excellence or virtue; κακία can mean badness or vice. In an allegory, abstract terms become speakers. Capitalization in an English translation can signal that personification, but it does not turn the scene into history.
Choose translations that fit the argument. “Excellence” can emphasize achievement; “virtue” can emphasize moral quality. Neither English word covers every Greek context by itself.

sections.title: 1. Pointing: οὗτος and ἐκεῖνος
body: ὅδε, ἥδε, τόδε points to “this here,” often something being introduced. οὗτος points to “this” person or thing, often something just mentioned; ἐκεῖνος points to “that,” often more remote. Their gender, number, and case follow their role and any noun they describe.
With a noun and article, the demonstrative normally stands outside the article–noun group: οὗτος ὁ βίος or ὁ βίος οὗτος. Without a noun it can stand on its own.

sections.title: 2. Asking: τίς and τί
body: Accented τίς asks “who?” or “which?”; neuter τί asks “what?” A question word can be a pronoun on its own or an adjective with a noun. The case shows its function: τίνα βίον αἱρεῖ; “Which life do you choose?”
Ask separately about the subject and the object. τίς αἱρεῖται; asks who chooses. τί αἱρεῖται; asks what someone chooses. The written question mark in Greek is a semicolon-shaped sign.

sections.title: 3. Someone, something, a certain
body: Indefinite τις/τι means “someone/something” or “a certain/some” with a noun. It is enclitic: its accent normally depends on neighboring words. Unlike interrogative τίς, it does not itself ask a question.

The forms largely match the interrogative but accentuation differs. Learn the distinction in context rather than assuming every written accent belongs to a question: enclitic accent rules can give an indefinite an accent in certain positions.

sections.title: 4. Where, how, and why?
body: Question adverbs do not decline: ποῦ asks “where?”, πόθεν “from where?”, ποῖ “to where?”, πῶς “how?”, and πότε “when?” Their indefinite partners include που, ποθεν, ποι, πως, ποτε.

In the Heracles story, questions help expose a promise: how does a way of life produce its rewards, and from where do necessities come? διὰ τί asks “why?” These are reading tools, not a new conditional or subjunctive system.

sections.title: Meet a story inside the Memorabilia
body: In Memorabilia 2.1.21–34, Xenophon’s Socrates retells a story attributed to Prodicus. The young Heracles encounters two personified ways of life. The episode is a moral allegory embedded in a Socratic conversation, not a report of a historical meeting.

Think of the four books as a gallery of encounters rather than a continuous biography. Book 1 answers accusations against Socrates and presents his religious practice and daily conduct. Books 2–3 explore family, friendship, useful work, and leadership. Book 4 gives sustained attention to education, including the questioning of Euthydemus. The movement from an ordinary habit to a public responsibility is characteristic of the collection.

Xenophon writes as an advocate for a teacher condemned at Athens in 399 BCE. His Socrates improves other people through example, questions, and practical reasoning. That organizing purpose makes the work valuable evidence for an ancient interpretation of Socrates; it does not make every conversation a stenographic record. Notice who asks the questions, who changes position, and where the narrator supplies the judgment.

Reading invitation: open Book 1, chapter 5, then Book 4, chapter 5. Ask whether mastery of appetite is merely a rule about pleasure or a condition for learning and dependable action. Keep a small dossier of the different kinds of evidence Xenophon offers: reported speech, observed habit, analogy, and the narrator’s praise.

Our simplified reading keeps the competing promises and the relation between effort and worthwhile achievement. It does not reproduce Prodicus’s original wording. The chain matters: Prodicus is credited with the story, Socrates tells it in Xenophon’s work, and the course adapts that account.

sections.title: A hero before the famous labors
body: The narrative asks the student to meet Heracles at a moment of choice. His future achievements have not yet answered the question for him. Personification lets competing arguments walk into the scene as characters.

The Reading banner uses a familiar heroic visual cue and two contrasting figures. It is an imagined allegorical scene. Clothing, gestures, and paths are visual interpretation; they are not evidence of an actual crossroads or a documented encounter. The Culture/History banner instead imagines a storyteller and listeners, inviting you to consider how an argument changes when it becomes a memorable tale.

sections.title: Interrogate the advertisement
body: Each way of life makes an attractive offer. Instead of deciding from costume or beauty, examine the promise: what must happen to make it true, whose work supports it, and what does the speaker leave out?

Create a short “claim and question” card. Put a tempting promise on one side and a question beginning “How?”, “From where?”, or “At whose expense?” on the other. Your job is to test reasoning rather than label every pleasure bad.

sections.title: Choice does not end the discussion
body: The story presents effort as part of worthy achievement. That does not mean every difficulty is useful or every easy action wrong. Compare this allegory with the actual need for food in the Armenian march in the next lesson.

Find a demonstrative that points to a proposed life and an interrogative that challenges it. Explain why “this” identifies a claim while “why?” asks for its justification. The small words carry much of the debate.
